cases.answer:
Short answer
Traditionally, Mars in the 10th house is associated with public activity, courage/valour, energetic or forceful achievement in career, and a role in “service” (typically a middle-level position via peers/equals) — with results depending on benefic aspects and the condition of other 10th-house factors. (Citations below.)

Supporting points with citations
- Courage, heroism, ability to accomplish great undertakings: Phaladeepika says that if the Sun or Mars occupy the 10th house, “the native will be a great and mighty personage … he will be able to accomplish great undertakings involving much valour and heroism” (Passage 2 — Phaladeepika, Ch.16, sl.28). This is DIRECT TEXT.
- Liked by people / public standing: The same Phaladeepika sloka explicitly adds that such a native is “liked by the people” (Passage 2). DIRECT TEXT.
- Career/service role and rank nuance: Brihat Jataka states that when Sun, Mars or Saturn occupy the 10th house without a benefic aspect, the person will be “in service,” and distinguishes degrees — the Sun indicates high-grade service, Mars a middle position, Saturn a low order (Passage 5 — Brihat Jataka, Ch.23, sl.17). DIRECT TEXT. From this you can traditionally synthesize that Mars in 10th often points to an active, middling professional role connected with peers/equals rather than a highest-level post (TRADITIONAL SYNTHESIS).
- Importance of benefic influence / context: Several Parasara passages emphasize that the 10th’s results change strongly when benefics or malefics occupy/aspect the 10th or its lord (Passage 1 and Passage 3 — Brihat Parasara Hora Sastra, Ch.23). While those slokas discuss the 10th lord and combinations, the general lesson they give is that Mars’s basic 10th-house themes will be modified by accompanying planets and aspects (TRADITIONAL SYNTHESIS based on cited passages).

Limitations
- The retrieved passages give general thematic results for Mars in the 10th and for planets in the 10th without benefic aspect. They do not specify exact professions, precise rank in every case, or timing — those would require additional chart details (e.g., aspects, strength of Mars, condition of the 10th lord) which are not present in the supplied material.

No fabricated chart facts, no guaranteed career/fame claims, and relies on retrieved evidence with correct attributions and scope limits.

Short answer
- BPHS links Venus in the 7th house with partnership/wife matters and a strong increase in sexual/romantic desire — traditionally described as “excessive lust.” (DIRECT TEXT: Passage 2; Passage 4/5.)
- Cautions BPHS explicitly gives: if Venus in the 7th is joined by malefics it can cause serious harm to the wife (even phrased as causing the wife's death); the condition (strength, debilitation, combustion, conjunctions or aspects) of the 7th-lord/venus changes outcomes (good if strong and aspected by benefics; bad if weak/debilitated/combusted). (DIRECT TEXT: Passage 4/5.)

Supporting points (traditional synthesis)
1. Venus as 7th-house factor: BPHS lists Venus under the significations of the 7th (wife/partnership) — so Venus in the 7th emphasizes the house’s marital/partner themes. (Passage 2 — Brihat Parasara Hora Sastra, Ch.34, Sloka 7.)
2. Increased sexual/romantic drive: BPHS explicitly says when Venus is placed in the 7th the native will be excessively lustful; the 7th and Venus share the same sexual/partner quality so the quality is amplified. (Passage 4/5 — Ch.20, Effects of the Seventh House.)
3. Severe caution about malefics and planet-strength: BPHS warns that if Venus (or a planet in the 7th) is with malefics, the combination can cause the death of the wife; and that the positive or negative results depend strongly on the strength and associations of the 7th-lord (strong + benefic = happiness, weak/debilitated/combust = sickly wife, multiple wives, etc.). Those are cited as explicit conditional outcomes in the text. (Passage 4/5 — Ch.20, Slokas 3–6 and notes.)
4. Practical implication: taken together, BPHS treats Venus-in-7th as signifying strong partner/sexual energy but also as a placement that needs careful examination of conjunctions, aspects and planetary strength before making favorable or unfavorable predictions. (Passage 4/5 — Ch.20; synthesis from Passage 2.)

Limitation / caution about what is not established here
- BPHS statements above specify conditional outcomes (depend on malefics, strength, aspects). You would need the chart details about whether Venus is conjoined by malefics/benefics, its strength (own/exaltation/debilitation/combustion) and the 7th‑lord’s condition to decide which of these outcomes is likely. The supplied facts only give “Venus in house 7,” so we can reliably state the themes and the cautions BPHS prescribes, but not which particular result will occur in this chart.

Short answer
BPHS (Bṛhat Parāśara) links the 5th‑lord’s house and the placement/strength of Jupiter directly to issues about children. Key points the text gives:

Direct text (quoted/paraphrased from the cited slokas)
- The 5th‑lord placed in a kendra or trikona (or in the 5th itself) brings thorough happiness from sons; the 5th‑lord in the 6th, 8th or 12th is to be predicted as producing a thorough lack of sons (Passage 3 — Ch.18, sl.1–3).  (DIRECT TEXT)
- If the 5th‑lord is in the 6th House, and the Ascendant‑lord is conjunct Mars, the firstborn may die and the wife may become unable to conceive thereafter (kakbandhya) — an example and statement in the text (Passage 3 — Ch.18, sl.4 with examples). (DIRECT TEXT)
- If the debilitated 5th‑lord is in the 12th, 6th or 8th, or if Mercury and Ketu are in the 5th, the wife may be kakbandhya (sterile after one child) and the 5th‑house is extremely weakened (Passage 3 — Ch.18, sl.5–7). (DIRECT TEXT)
- The 5th‑lord relegated to the 6th means the native’s sons will be “equal to his enemies” (hostile), may die, or the native may acquire an adopted/purchased son (Passage 4 — Ch.26, sl.54). (DIRECT TEXT)
- Specific to Jupiter: the text gives child‑number formulas tied to Jupiter’s condition. For example, when Jupiter is in highest exaltation the number of children may be nine; and when Jupiter is placed in the 5th (the text also mentions “in the 5th or the Sth[?] House”) the 5th‑lord is strengthened and a particular number (eight, the Vasus) is indicated in that scenario (Passage 1 — Ch.18, sl.24–32). (DIRECT TEXT)

Traditional synthesis (combining the chart factors described by BPHS)
- Jupiter’s good placement or exaltation supports progeny (Passage 1), while a weak or debased 5th‑lord (placed in trik/3/6/8/12 or combust/with malefics) obstructs children or causes death/sterility (Passage 3, Passage 4). (TRADITIONAL SYNTHESIS)
- When the 5th‑lord occupies the 6th, expect obstacles to issues from disease, hostility, or adoption as remedies/outcomes (Passage 4, Passage 3). (TRADITIONAL SYNTHESIS)

Notes and limits
- The slokas give several specific conditional formulas (numbers of children, kakbandhya, adopted sons) tied to combinations of the 5th‑lord, Jupiter, malefics, Mercury/Ketu, and Mars. I have only cited the passages you supplied. BPHS treats these as conditional rules — the exact outcome depends on the whole chart and other modifying factors not listed here. (LIMITATION)

cases.answer:
Direct answer
- Brihat Parasara (BPHS) states that when Jupiter (the significator of wealth, guru) is placed in the 2nd house (the house of wealth) the native will be wealthy — i.e., Jupiter in the 2nd is a wealth-giving placement. (Passage 1 — Brihat Parasara Hora Sastra, Ch. 15, sloka 3; PDF p. 209–211.) — EVIDENCE LEVEL: DIRECT TEXT.

Supporting notes from the same material
- BPHS explicitly contrasts its view with some other authors (e.g., Chamatkar Chintamani / Bhava Kutuhala) who claim Jupiter in the 2nd forces hard, insecure earning. BPHS rejects that negative reading and declares Jupiter-in-2nd to be wealth-giving (Passage 1 — Ch. 15, notes). — EVIDENCE LEVEL: DIRECT TEXT / TRADITIONAL SYNTHESIS.

Minor related points (not required to answer but present in the retrieved material)
- BPHS also notes that Jupiter together with Mars in the 2nd supports wealth (Passage 1, sloka 3). (Passage 1 — Ch. 15.) — EVIDENCE LEVEL: DIRECT TEXT.
- A different discussion about the 2nd from Karakamsha treats Jupiter’s effects there differently (fame, daughters, and certain behavioural tendencies); that is a separate rule and not the same as “Jupiter in the 2nd house” from the lagna (Passage 5 — Ch. 35). — EVIDENCE LEVEL: DIRECT TEXT.

Summary sentence
- In short: according to BPHS, Jupiter placed in the 2nd house traditionally indicates wealth and makes the native wealthy (BPHS explicitly rejects the contrary claim found in some other texts).

Short answer
- Brihat Parashara Hora Shastra (BPHS) treats the 11th bhava as the primary house of gains, and gives clear rules about when gains will be produced or frustrated. (See Passages 1–5 below.)

Key BPHS points (with cited passages and brief practical meaning)

1) Strong placement of the 11th‑lord = gains
- DIRECT TEXT: “When the 11th Lord is situated in the 11th House itself or in an angle or in a trine … the combination will bring many gains to the native.” (Passage 3 — BPHS Ch.24 Sloka 2).  
- Practical reading (Traditional synthesis): If the 11th‑lord is placed in good houses (11th, kendras, trines) or is exalted, the chart is classically promised many and special gains.

2) Specific favourable configurations producing large gains
- DIRECT TEXT: BPHS gives examples where placements of Jupiter and other bhava‑lords produce very large wealth (numbers of Nishkas) at certain years — e.g., 11th occupied by Jupiter, 2nd by Moon, 9th by Venus → possessor of 6000 Nishkas; other slokas mention gains in 33rd, 36th, 40th years when lord placements are favourable. (Passage 1 — Ch.24 Slokas 3–8).  
- Practical synthesis: BPHS uses these configurations to show that particular combinations of bhava‑lords and benefics in the 11th/related houses are associated with measurable gains and timed increases in fortune.

3) Benefics in the 11th or benefic aspects bring gains; malefics cause mixed results and expenses
- DIRECT TEXT: If benefics aspect the 11th (or Lagna‑Pada), earnings will be abundant; malefics produce gains through foul means or mixed planets produce mixed (fair + foul) results; such aspects also indicate higher expenses. (Passage 4 — Ch.31 Slokas 16–17).  
- Practical synthesis: The moral/quality source of gains (fair vs foul) and the net effect (net gain vs high expenses) depend on whether benefics or malefics influence the 11th.

4) Placements that block or produce losses
- DIRECT TEXT: If the 11th Lord is in debilitation, in combustion, or occupies the 6th, 8th, or 12th with a malefic, then “the native does not have any gain in spite of excessive efforts.” (Passage 1 — Ch.24 Sloka 11).  
- DIRECT TEXT: If the 12th Lord is placed in the 11th House, the native will incur losses; gains are frustrated or meagre and may come from others. (Passage 5 — Ch.26 Sloka 143).  
- Practical synthesis: BPHS warns that ill‑placed 11th‑lord or presence of the house’s natural enemy (12th‑lord in 11th) undermines expected gains.

5) Secondary note: bhava‑lordal placements into 11th carry theme of that bhava into gains
- DIRECT TEXT: Example — “In case the 5th Lord occupies the 11th House, the native will be learned, dear to the people, an illustrious author, very skilful and endowed with many sons and wealth.” (Passage 2 — Ch.26 Sloka 59).  
- Practical synthesis: When a house‑lord occupies the 11th, the affairs of that house tend to express themselves through gains and social returns.

Concise summary
- BPHS: the 11th is the house of gains; a well‑placed 11th‑lord (in 11th, angles, trines, exaltation) and benefic influence give clear and often large gains (Passages 1,3,4). Specific combinations of bhava lords and benefics are described as producing substantial wealth at particular times (Passage 1). Conversely, an afflicted or debilitated 11th‑lord, or the 12th‑lord in the 11th, or malefic influences, will frustrate gains or create losses (Passages 1,5).

Limitations / what BPHS does not establish here
- BPHS in these slokas gives qualitative rules and some illustrative numeric examples (Nishkas) and ages; it does not give a single formula that applies universally to every birth without checking the whole chart (planetary dignity, aspects, dasha, divisional charts). The passages above are the specific BPHS statements relevant to 11th‑house gains included in your retrieved material.

Short answer
- In Brihat Jataka the passages that mention Saturn in Kumbha (Aquarius) are describing Rajayoga (conditions producing kingship or sovereign power) — i.e., combinations that can make a native a king or powerful ruler when Saturn is in Aquarius together with specific placements of other planets. (See Sloka 4 and Sloka 13–14 of Chapter 11 in Brihat Jataka.) — DIRECT TEXT (Passages 2 and 4).

What the Brihat Jataka text actually says (with sources)
- Brihat Jataka, Ch. 11 Sloka 4 (Passage 2 — PDF p. 260–261): Varaha‑mihira lists a set of placements including “Saturn in Kumbha (Aquarius), the Sun in Mesha (Aries), the Moon in Vrishabha (Taurus), Mercury in Mithuna (Gemini), Jupiter in Simha (Leo), and Mars in Vrischika (Scorpio)” and says that with those placements (and certain Lagnas) “three Rajayogas arise.” The sloka is explicitly naming Saturn-in-Aquarius as part of a Rajayoga formula. — DIRECT TEXT (Passage 2).

- Brihat Jataka, Ch. 11 Slokas 13–14 (Passage 4 — PDF p. 271–275): Varahamihira gives the general rule that when three or more planets occupy their own signs or exaltation and are simultaneously trine to one another (i.e., form benefic trinal placements), the native becomes a king if born to a royal family; with five or more such planets even an ordinary-born person may become a king. Passage 14 then gives an example in which Saturn in Kumbha (Aquarius) is one of the planets in the exaltation/own-sign trine that produces kingship. — DIRECT TEXT (Passage 4).

Traditional synthesis (how these two slokas relate)
- Both slokas in Brihat Jataka treat Saturn-in-Aquarius as a potentially royalizing factor when it appears in specific powerful combinations with other planets (either the explicit planetary set named in Sloka 4 or as part of the “planets in own/exaltation signs forming trines” rule in Sloka 13–14). The text therefore uses Saturn in Kumbha as a contributing factor in Rajayoga formations. — TRADITIONAL SYNTHESIS (Passages 2 and 4).

Caveat from the text
- The Brihat Jataka rule ties the result to the overall combination (which planets, their signs, Lagnas, and number of exalted/own planets). Sloka 13 explicitly qualifies the outcome by family: “if born to a royal family, become kings; if five or more such planets, even ordinary families become kings; otherwise wealthy but not kings.” So Saturn in Aquarius alone is not claimed to guarantee kingship — it appears as part of larger Rajayoga configurations. — DIRECT TEXT / TRADITIONAL SYNTHESIS (Passage 4).

cases.answer:
Brihat Jataka (Ch. 8, sloka 17) states that during Venus’s dasa, when Venus is auspicious the native will enjoy many sensual and material pleasures and gains. (Passage 5 — Brihat Jataka.)

Directly stated benefits listed include:
- Pleasure in music, sensual enjoyments, fragrant perfumes, fine food and drink, and good clothing. (Passage 5)
- Association with women, jewels, splendour and other luxuries that kindle sexual appetite. (Passage 5)
- Acquisition of knowledge and fulfilment of desired objects; many friends. (Passage 5)
- Skill in trade and agriculture; success in buying and selling. (Passage 5)
- Receipt of hidden treasure and significant acquisition of wealth. (Passage 5)

(Brihat Jataka also notes the converse: if Venus is inauspicious in its dasa, the person may suffer troubles from friends and opponents — see the same passage.)
